subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: In the cavern beneath the mere, Beowulf's own sword failed him, unable to bite the hide of Grendel's mother. The monster bore him down and drew a knife, and only his mail-coat saved his life. Then Beowulf saw upon the wall a great sword forged by giants, too heavy for any ordinary man, and seizing it he struck the monster's neck and killed her. He found Grendel's corpse and cut off its head, and the giant blade melted away in the monster's hot and venomous blood.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: When a war between gods cracked one of the pillars holding up the sky, the heavens tilted and tore, fires raged and floods poured through the gap. The goddess Nuwa took pity on the suffering world. She gathered stones of five colors, melted them in a great fire, and patched the broken sky with the molten paste. To prop up the fallen corner she cut the legs from a giant turtle and set them as new pillars at the four directions, and so she repaired the world a second time after she had made it.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: The triumph over Grendel was brief, for the next night Grendel's mother came to avenge her son, a monstrous water-hag who carried off one of Hrothgar's dearest counselors. Beowulf followed her trail to a dark and dreadful mere, and plunged fully armed into its haunted waters. He sank for the better part of a day before reaching the bottom, where the monster dragged him to her cavern, and there, in a hall beneath the lake, the hero fought her for his life.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Anansi was famous for his bottomless greed, and one tale tells how he wished to keep an entire pot of beans for himself rather than share it with his family. He hid the hot pot under his cap, claiming he had simply taken a vow of silence and could not eat. The beans steamed and scalded his scalp, and when he could bear it no longer he tore the cap away. The boiling beans had cooked every hair from his head, and that, the storytellers say, is why the spider is bald to this day.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Long ago all the stories in the world belonged to the sky god Nyame, and there were no tales for people to tell. Anansi the spider climbed to the sky and asked to buy them, and Nyame, amused, set an impossible price: the spider must capture the python that swallows men whole, the leopard with terrible teeth, the hornets that sting like fire, and the unseen fairy who fears no enemy. Anansi, small and clever, accepted, and by his cunning won them all.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The new city of Rome had warriors but no women, and the neighboring tribes refused to allow their daughters to marry such a band of outlaws. Romulus devised a stratagem. He invited the Sabines to a great festival, and at a signal the Roman men seized the unmarried Sabine women and carried them off. The Sabines returned in war, but when the two armies met, the abducted women, now wives and mothers, threw themselves between the lines, begging their fathers and husbands to make peace.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: The fairy Mmoatia was the hardest of Nyame's four prizes, for she was a creature no one could see. Anansi carved a small wooden doll, coated it with sticky gum, and set a bowl of mashed yams in its lap beside a forest path. When the fairy came and the doll did not answer her polite greeting, she struck it in anger and her hand stuck fast. She struck again with the other hand, then kicked, until she was caught entirely, glued to the silent doll by her own temper.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: The musician Orpheus, who had lost his wife Eurydice twice to the underworld, never loved again, and his grief turned him away from all women. The frenzied followers of Dionysus, the Maenads, took offense at his rejection and his sorrow, and in their wild rage they fell upon him and tore him apart. His severed head, still singing, floated down the river to the sea, and the Muses gathered the scattered pieces of the poet and buried them, while his lyre was set among the stars.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: Haitian folk tradition tells of the lwa, the spirits served in Vodou, who are organized into families or nanchon and act as intermediaries between humanity and the distant creator. Papa Legba stands at the crossroads and the gateway, and like Esu of the Yoruba he must be greeted first, for he opens the way between the worlds. The Gede spirits, presided over by the irreverent Baron Samedi, govern death and the cemetery, and their rites mingle mourning with bawdy laughter and a fierce embrace of life.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: When Heracles undertook his final labor, the capture of Cerberus, he first had to be initiated into the sacred mysteries so that he might enter the land of the dead and return alive. Guided by Hermes and Athena, he descended through the cave at Taenarum. In the underworld he met the shade of Meleager and promised to marry his sister, freed Theseus from the Chair of Forgetfulness, and even wounded Hades himself in the shoulder before wrestling the great hound into submission and dragging it up to the light.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: Hawaiian legend tells of the menehune, a small and industrious people who lived in the forests and worked only by night. They were said to be master builders, able to complete a great fishpond, a temple, or a watercourse in a single night, working in long lines that passed the stones from hand to hand. If a task was not finished before dawn, the menehune would abandon it forever, and certain unfinished ancient structures were pointed out as proof of their interrupted labors.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The Romans honored a goddess Vesta, the keeper of the hearth, and her sacred flame burned perpetually in her round temple in the Forum. Six priestesses, the Vestal Virgins, tended the fire and were bound to chastity for thirty years of service. If the flame went out, it was taken as a dreadful omen of danger to the state, and the negligent priestess was scourged. A Vestal who broke her vow of chastity faced a far worse fate, being entombed alive in a small underground chamber.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The Levantine myth of Baal, the storm god who brought the rains, told of his struggle against Mot, the god of death and the parched dry season. Mot swallowed Baal, and the storm god descended into the underworld, and without him the rains failed and the earth cracked and withered. Baal's sister, the fierce goddess Anat, hunted down Mot and destroyed him, grinding him like grain, and Baal returned to life, the rains came again, and the fertility of the land was restored.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: Raven, on the northern coast, was forever hungry, and his greed drove the plot of many tales. In one, Raven tricked the sea-folk out of their store of fish, in another he stole a fisherman's catch by playing dead so convincingly that the man tossed his apparent carcass into the boat among the salmon. The trickster's appetite was bottomless, and though his schemes sometimes benefited the people, they were never undertaken for the people's sake; the world was simply shaped by the side effects of Raven feeding himself.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Harpies were winged spirits, part woman and part bird, the snatchers who carried things away on sudden gusts of wind. They tormented the blind prophet Phineus, who had been cursed so that every time food was set before him, the Harpies swooped down to seize it or to befoul it, leaving him to starve in sight of plenty. The winged sons of the North Wind, sailing with the Argonauts, at last drove the Harpies off, and Phineus, freed from the curse, repaid his rescuers with prophecy.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: The doom of Camelot lay coiled within its own splendor. Lancelot, the noblest knight of the Round Table, and Queen Guinevere fell into a love that honor could not sanction, and when their secret was at last dragged into the open, the fellowship split into warring factions. Arthur was forced to condemn his queen and make war upon his dearest friend, and while the king was abroad with his armies, his nephew Mordred seized the throne and the realm fell into ruin.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The European wonder tale almost always begins with a lack or a wrong: a king with no heir, a child stolen, a princess cursed, a family in poverty. This opening misfortune sets the hero on a journey, and the tale will not close until the lack has been filled and the wrong righted. Folklorists found that beneath the endless variety of these stories lay a small and remarkably stable set of functions, a hidden grammar that gave the wonder tale its satisfying and recognizable shape.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: A widespread Andean tale tells of a llama herder who noticed his animals behaving strangely, refusing to graze and gazing up at the night sky in distress. When he questioned the llamas, they warned him that a great flood was coming to drown the world. The herder gathered his family and all the animals he could and climbed to the top of a high mountain. The waters rose almost to the peak, and when at last they receded, the herder and his charges descended to repopulate the emptied land.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: The legend of Melusine spread through medieval France and beyond, telling of a beautiful woman who agreed to marry a nobleman on one condition: that he never look upon her on a Saturday. For years they prospered and she bore him many children, until at last his curiosity or jealousy overcame him. Spying on her in her bath, he saw that from the waist down she had the tail of a serpent. The secret broken, Melusine cried out, transformed fully into a dragon, and flew from the castle forever.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: The Caribbean folktale often opens and closes with a formula, the storyteller calling out a cry and the listeners answering, a ritual that gathers the audience and marks the passage into the world of the tale. The teller might announce that this is not a true story, or warn that the tale itself is a lie, and end by sending the story away on a journey or claiming to have been kicked out of the events described. These framing devices made the telling itself a small performed ceremony.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: At the festival of Samhain, the boundary between the human world and the Otherworld grew thin, and the sidhe rode abroad in great processions. Mortals left offerings of food and milk to placate the fairy host, and travelers feared being swept up by the Wild Hunt or led astray by lights dancing over the bog. The dead, too, could return on this night, and the living masked themselves so that no wandering spirit or fairy would recognize and claim them.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The founder of the Goguryeo kingdom was Jumong, a legendary archer whose name meant skilled bowman. His mother was a daughter of a river god, impregnated by sunlight, and Jumong was born from an egg. Persecuted by jealous princes, he fled south on horseback, and when a river blocked his escape, he called out his divine ancestry, and fish and turtles rose to the surface and formed a living bridge so that he could cross. On the far side he founded the kingdom that would become one of the great powers of the peninsula.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The legend of the kelpie haunted the lochs and rivers of Scotland with a particular dread. In the ballad and folk traditions the water horse was a shape-shifting predator, appearing as a fine gray or black horse to tempt a rider, and especially eager to drown children who climbed playfully onto its lengthening back. Some tales said the kelpie could also take the form of a handsome man, and that a woman who noticed waterweed in her suitor's hair had narrowly escaped a watery death.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: Tir na nOg, the Land of the Young, lay across the western sea, a country where no one aged, no one sickened, and the trees bore fruit and blossom at once. The warrior-poet Oisin was carried there by the fairy woman Niamh of the Golden Hair and lived in joy for what seemed three years. When he longed to see Ireland again, Niamh warned him never to let his foot touch mortal soil, but a fall from his horse aged him three hundred years in an instant, for that was the true span he had been away.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The Tain Bo Cuailnge, the Cattle Raid of Cooley, is the central epic of the Ulster Cycle, and it begins with a quarrel in bed. Queen Medb of Connacht and her husband Ailill compared their possessions and found themselves perfectly matched, until Ailill produced a magnificent white-horned bull that had no equal in Medb's herds. To restore the balance and her pride, Medb resolved to win the great brown bull of Cooley, by purchase if she could and by war if she must.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: In the Maori account of creation, the sky father Ranginui and the earth mother Papatuanuku lay locked in a tight embrace, and their children were crushed in the darkness between them. The children debated whether to kill their parents or to part them, and at last Tane, the god of forests, lay on his back and pushed with his powerful legs until sky and earth were forced apart. Light flooded into the world, but Ranginui's tears still fall as rain, and the mists rising from the ground are Papatuanuku sighing for her lost husband.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The German legend of Faust tells of a learned scholar who, dissatisfied with the limits of human knowledge and pleasure, makes a pact with the devil's emissary Mephistopheles. In exchange for years of magical power, forbidden knowledge, and every worldly delight, Faust pledges his immortal soul. The legend, rooted in tales of a real wandering magician, became one of the great myths of Europe, a warning about the price of ambition and the dangerous hunger to know and possess everything.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: The pilgrims faced eighty-one calamities on the road to the west, for the journey had to be hard if the scriptures were to be earned. They met demons who wished to eat the flesh of the holy monk to gain immortality, kingdoms ruled by sorcerers, mountains of fire, and rivers that could not be crossed. Again and again Sun Wukong used his cunning and his transformations to defeat the monsters, sometimes calling upon the gods of heaven for aid, and the company moved on toward their distant goal.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Heimdall's horn would sound the alarm of Ragnarok. The watchman of the gods, who needed no more sleep than a bird and could see for a hundred leagues by day or night, kept the Gjallarhorn ready at the foot of the rainbow bridge. When he saw the forces of chaos massing for the assault on Asgard, he would lift the horn to his lips and blow a blast so loud it would ring through all the nine worlds, and every god and every fallen warrior in Valhalla would know the final hour had come.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The pre-Islamic and Islamic folklore of the Near East was full of the jinn, beings created from smokeless fire as humans were created from clay. The jinn lived in a parallel society with their own tribes and faiths, mostly unseen but able to take many shapes. They might haunt deserts, ruins, and bathhouses, help or harm a person according to their nature, and the ifrit and the marid were named among their most powerful and fearsome kinds.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: Folk belief held that a person could be marked for vampirism from the very beginning of life. A child born with a caul, born with teeth, born on an unlucky day, or conceived during a forbidden time of the church calendar was thought to be at risk of rising after death. So too were those who had been excommunicated, who had practiced sorcery, or over whose corpse an animal had been allowed to leap. The vampire of folklore was, in part, a way of explaining the unquiet dead and the misfortunes of the living.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: In the beginning there was only Ginnungagap, the yawning void, with fire-world Muspelheim to the south and ice-world Niflheim to the north. Where their heat and rime met, the frost dripped into life and the primal giant Ymir took shape. From his slain body the gods Odin, Vili, and Ve fashioned the earth: his flesh the soil, his blood the seas, his skull the dome of the sky. Through all the nine worlds stretched Yggdrasil, the great ash whose roots a serpent gnawed and whose branches an eagle crowned.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The incantation bowls of late antique Mesopotamia are a vivid trace of Near Eastern folk demonology. These simple clay bowls were inscribed in spiraling lines of script with protective spells, often naming the demons to be bound and the angels called to drive them away, and sometimes drawn with the image of a chained demon at the center. Buried upside down beneath the threshold or the corners of a house, they were meant to trap any evil spirit that tried to enter.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Vietnamese tradition traces the origin of the people to a union of a dragon and a fairy. The dragon lord Lac Long Quan, a being of the water, married the mountain fairy Au Co, and she bore a sac containing one hundred eggs, from which one hundred children hatched. Because the dragon belonged to the lowlands and the sea and the fairy to the highlands, the parents parted, each taking fifty children, and from these children descended the Vietnamese people, the offspring of dragon and immortal.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: At Ragnarok the great wolf Fenrir, bound long ago by the gods with a magic fetter, would finally break free. His lower jaw would scrape the earth and his upper jaw the sky, and fire would burn from his eyes and nostrils. Odin, the All-Father, would ride out to meet him, and despite all his wisdom and his deathless spear, the wolf would swallow the chief of the gods whole. Then Odin's son Vidar would step forward to avenge his father, tearing the wolf's jaws apart with his great boot.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A folktale from West Africa tells why the sky is far from the earth. Long ago the sky hung low, and people could simply break off a piece of it to eat, for the sky itself was food. But the people grew wasteful and greedy, breaking off far more than they could eat and throwing the rest away. The sky, offended by the waste of its generous gift, rose higher and higher out of reach, and from that day people had to labor in the fields for their bread.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The domovoi is the guardian spirit of the Slavic household, a small bearded man who dwells behind the stove or beneath the threshold. A well-treated domovoi protects the family, keeps the livestock healthy, and warns of coming trouble by moaning or rattling in the night. He demands respect and small offerings of bread and salt, and when a family moved house they would coax their domovoi to follow, carrying embers from the old hearth so the protective spirit would not be left behind.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The Romans told how the hero Horatius Cocles held the wooden bridge across the Tiber alone against an entire invading army. While his comrades hacked the bridge down behind him, Horatius stood his ground in the narrow gap, holding off the enemy with his sword and shield. When the timbers finally crashed into the river, Horatius, fully armored, plunged into the current and swam to safety, and the city was saved by the courage of a single man who would not yield his ground.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: To eat the food of the Otherworld was to bind oneself to it forever. Many tales warn of mortals who stumbled into a fairy feast, a hall blazing with light and music in the heart of a lonely hill, and accepted a single cup or a bite of bread. Those who ate could never fully return to the human world; they wandered home decades later untouched by age, or never came home at all. The wise refused every offered dish, no matter how their hunger gnawed at them.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: The curse of the gold worked its ruin through deception. At the court of the Burgundians, Sigurd was given a potion of forgetfulness, and his memory of Brynhild was wiped away. He married the princess Gudrun, and then, not knowing what he did, he used a shape-shifting spell to pass through Brynhild's wall of fire in the guise of another man, so that she would marry that man instead. By this magic Sigurd unknowingly betrayed the woman he had loved, and the seeds of catastrophe were sown.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A folktale from across Africa explains why dogs live with people while their wild cousins remain in the bush. Long ago the dog and the jackal, or the dog and the wolf, set out together one cold night, and the dog followed the scent of woodsmoke to a human campfire and its warmth and scraps of food. The wild cousin would not come near the fire and the noise of people, and so the dog stayed with humankind and the jackal kept to the wilderness, and so it has been ever since.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: Germanic tradition told of the Wild Hunt, a spectral procession of huntsmen, hounds, and horses that swept through the winter sky and the storm. The hunt was led by a great figure, sometimes named as the god Wodan, sometimes as a damned soul or a legendary king. To see the Wild Hunt was an omen of catastrophe, war, plague, or one's own death, and a person caught in its path might be swept up into the chase or trampled, and so on the wild nights people stayed indoors and kept their eyes from the sky.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The night marchers, the huaka'i po, are among the most feared spirits of Hawaiian belief, the ghostly processions of ancient warriors who travel sacred paths on certain nights. They are heralded by the sound of drums and conch shells and the glow of torches, and to look upon them or to stand in their path is said to bring death. Hawaiian custom held that a person caught in the way of the night marchers should lie face down on the ground and show no disrespect, hoping a marching ancestor would claim them as kin.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: Vainamoinen, the central hero of the Kalevala, was no warrior but a sage and a singer, born already old and wise from the womb of Ilmatar after centuries within her. His power lay in song and the knowledge of origins, for in Finnish belief, to know the true beginning of any thing was to command it. With his songs he could raise storms, calm seas, and sink a rival into a bog up to his very chin, and his voice was the deepest magic in the world.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The kitsune is the fox spirit of Japanese folklore, and the older it grows the more tails it sprouts, until at nine hundred years it possesses nine and shines with a golden or white coat. A kitsune can take human form, most often a beautiful woman, to deceive or to repay a kindness. Stories tell of fox-wives who lived happily with mortal husbands for years, bore them children, and vanished only when a barking dog or a careless word revealed the tail they could never fully hide.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A folktale from southern Africa tells why the hare has a split lip. The moon sent the hare to carry a message of comfort to humankind, that just as the moon dies and is reborn, so people would die and live again. But the careless hare muddled the message and told people instead that they would die and not return. Furious at the error that brought death's finality to humankind, the moon struck the hare across the mouth, and the hare's lip has been split ever since.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Burmese tradition reveres the nats, a host of spirits venerated alongside the dominant religion. Many of the most important nats are the spirits of real people who died violent or tragic deaths and whose restless power had to be honored and contained. The thirty-seven great nats each have their own legend of a life cut short by execution, accident, or grief, and shrines to them stand in homes and at sacred sites, the spirits propitiated with offerings so that their lingering power protects rather than harms.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: Not all the Titans fought against Zeus, and not all were punished. Prometheus, whose name meant forethought, had foreseen the outcome and sided with the Olympians, and so he kept his freedom for a time. The Titan Atlas, however, had led the enemy forces, and for this Zeus condemned him to a punishment without end: to stand at the western edge of the world and bear the weight of the heavens upon his shoulders forever, keeping sky and earth apart.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: Between two cliffs of a narrow strait lurked two monsters, and a sailor could not avoid both. On one side was Scylla, a creature with six long necks and six ravening heads, who snatched men from the decks of passing ships. On the other was Charybdis, a vast whirlpool that swallowed the sea three times a day and could drag a whole vessel down. Odysseus, warned by Circe, steered close to Scylla, judging it better to lose six men to her jaws than the entire ship to the whirlpool.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: Songlines, sometimes called dreaming tracks, are the routes across the Australian land travelled by the ancestral beings during the Dreaming. Each songline is recorded in a sequence of songs that describe the landmarks along the way, the waterholes, the ridges, the resting places. To sing the song in order is to know the path, and so the songlines served as both sacred narrative and a precise map, allowing knowledgeable travelers to cross vast and seemingly featureless country by following the words of the ancestors.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The English legend of Herne the Hunter placed a ghostly figure in the great forest of Windsor, a spectral huntsman wearing the antlers of a stag upon his head. He was said to ride out on stormy nights, leading a phantom hunt of baying hounds, and his appearance was an omen of misfortune for the realm. The legend, like the wider tradition of the Wild Hunt, gathered around the figure of the antlered hunter all the old dread of the forest, the storm, and the powers that moved through the night.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The Phrygian myth of Cybele and her young consort Attis was a tale of death, mourning, and renewal tied to the spring. Attis, a god of vegetation, died beneath a pine tree, and from his blood violets were said to spring. His cult mourned his death in early spring and then celebrated his return, and the pine tree, cut and carried in procession, became the symbol of the god whose dying and rising matched the bare winter and the greening of the new season.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: A Dreaming story of southeastern Australia tells how fire was once hoarded by the water-rat, or by a band of women, who kept it hidden and refused to share. Various tellings name a different hero, but the pattern holds: a clever ancestral being, often a bird, steals or tricks the fire away from those who selfishly kept it. The fire is then placed within the heart of certain trees, so that ever after people can draw it out by rubbing wood together, and warmth and cooking belong to everyone.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: To complete a magic spell, Vainamoinen needed three lost words of power, and he was told they could be found only in the belly of the dead giant Antero Vipunen. The hero journeyed to where the giant lay buried under the earth, trees growing from his shoulders, and forced his way into the giant's mouth. From within Vipunen's body Vainamoinen tormented him, forging iron in his stomach, until the giant, to be rid of his tormentor, sang out all the ancient words and origin-spells he had ever known.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: The Titanomachy was a war of ten years between the young gods led by Zeus and the older Titans led by Cronus. Neither side could gain the upper hand until Zeus, advised by Gaia, descended into Tartarus and freed the Cyclopes and the hundred-handed giants whom Uranus and Cronus had imprisoned. In gratitude the Cyclopes forged for Zeus his thunderbolts, for Poseidon his trident, and for Hades a helmet of invisibility, and with these weapons the tide of the war turned.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The transformation and its breaking lie at the heart of many wonder tales. A prince is bound in the shape of a frog, a bear, a serpent, a beast; a sister is turned into a bird, a brother into a deer. The spell can be broken only by a precise and difficult act of love or loyalty, a kiss freely given, a shirt of nettles sewn in silence, a year of patient suffering. When the enchantment lifts and the true form returns, the tale affirms that beneath every monstrous shape a worthy soul was waiting to be released.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: The swan maiden is a shapeshifter found in folktales across northern Europe. She and her sisters fly down to a lake, set aside their swan-feathered cloaks, and bathe as women. A watching man steals one cloak, and the maiden, unable to fly, becomes his wife. The story almost always ends the same way: years later she recovers the hidden feather garment, puts it on, and rises into the sky, sometimes calling her husband to follow on an impossible quest if he would win her back.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: The Book of the Dead was not a single scripture but a collection of spells, illustrations, and instructions written on papyrus and buried with the dead to guide them through the Duat. Among its passages was the Negative Confession, in which the soul stood before forty-two divine judges and denied each sin in turn: I have not stolen, I have not killed, I have not caused tears, I have not stopped the flow of water. To pass, the deceased had to know the name of every gate and every guardian.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: Lemminkainen was the reckless, charming, and womanizing hero of the Kalevala, forever rushing into danger his elders warned him against. Seeking the hand of a maiden of Pohjola, he was set deadly tasks, and in attempting to shoot the swan of the river of the dead, he was himself killed and his body cut to pieces and thrown into the dark waters. His mother, refusing to accept his death, raked the river until she had recovered every fragment, then sewed him back together and sang the life back into him.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: French folklore feared the loup-garou, and the Baltic and Slavic lands told of werewolves with their own variations. In some traditions the werewolf was not always a villain. Tales from the eastern Baltic spoke of werewolves who descended into hell to recover stolen crops and bring fertility back to the fields, fighting the witches who had carried it away. For these communities the man-wolf was a kind of agrarian champion, his nocturnal transformation a service to the harvest rather than a crime.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: Among the Yolngu people of Arnhem Land, the two Wagilag Sisters are central ancestral figures whose journey shaped the land and established sacred law and ceremony. As the sisters travelled, naming the plants and animals they encountered, they came upon the waterhole of the great Rainbow Serpent. The serpent rose, swallowed the sisters and their child, and later disgorged them, and from this powerful and dangerous encounter came the patterns of ritual that the Yolngu maintain to this day.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: Among many peoples of the western plains and plateaus, Coyote was the great trickster, a figure of appetite and folly whose blunders often shaped the world. When the people first emerged into the land, it was Coyote who scattered the stars across the sky in careless handfuls instead of placing them in their proper patterns, which is why the heavens are sprinkled with disorder. He stole fire for humankind, but he also drowned, burned, and fooled himself a hundred times, dying and returning in tale after tale.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: When the gods needed a great wall built around Asgard, a master builder offered to raise it within a single winter, asking as payment the sun, the moon, and the goddess Freyja. The gods, on Loki's advice, agreed, certain the task was impossible. But the builder's mighty stallion hauled stone so swiftly that the wall neared completion in time. To save Freyja, Loki transformed himself into a mare and lured the stallion away, and the wall was left unfinished and the giant's price unpaid.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, was two parts god and one part man, and in his arrogance he oppressed his own people until they cried out to the heavens. The gods answered by creating Enkidu, a wild man who lived among the beasts, to be his match and his counterweight. The two fought a tremendous battle in the streets of Uruk, and finding neither could defeat the other, they embraced as friends, and the great adventures of the king truly began.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Esu, sometimes called Elegua, is the Yoruba orisha of the crossroads, the messenger who carries words and offerings between humans and the other orishas. He is a trickster, unpredictable and quick to take offense, and no ritual can succeed unless Esu is honored first, for he holds the keys to the paths. One famous story tells how Esu walked a road wearing a cap that was black on one side and white on the other, then set two friends quarreling over its color until their friendship was destroyed.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The tale of the cowherd Niulang and the weaver girl Zhinu is among the most cherished of Chinese legends. Zhinu, a heavenly weaver, descended to earth and married the mortal cowherd, and they lived in happiness with their two children. But the Queen Mother of Heaven, displeased at the union of a goddess and a man, drew a great river of stars across the sky to part them. Once each year, on the seventh night of the seventh month, a bridge of magpies forms across the Milky Way and the lovers may meet for a single day.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The goddess Nuwa, with the body of a serpent and the face of a woman, grew lonely in the early world and resolved to make companions. She knelt by a riverbank and shaped little figures from the yellow clay, and each one came to life and danced around her. The work was slow, so she dipped a cord in the mud and flicked it, and the splattered droplets became people too. Thus, the legend says, the nobility were the carefully sculpted ones and the common folk were born from the scattered drops.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The most heartbreaking tale of the Shahnameh is that of Rostam and his son Sohrab. The two had never met, for Rostam left the boy's mother before his birth. Sohrab grew into a mighty warrior and went seeking his famous father, but fate set them on opposite sides of a war. They fought as strangers, and Rostam dealt the younger man a mortal wound. Only as Sohrab lay dying did he reveal a token his mother had given him, and Rostam understood, too late, that he had killed his own child.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A West African dilemma tale ends not with a moral but with an unanswered question put to the listeners. A father has three sons, and each performs a marvelous deed to save him: one foresaw the danger, one carried the family to safety, one fought off the threat. The storyteller asks which son deserves the inheritance, and the tale stops there. The audience must argue it out among themselves, and the story becomes a tool for teaching judgment, debate, and the weighing of competing claims.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The myth of Adonis, beloved of Aphrodite and adopted from Near Eastern tradition, told of a beautiful youth killed by a wild boar, from whose blood the red anemone flower sprang. After his death, a compromise among the gods allowed Adonis to spend part of the year in the underworld and part in the world above. Women planted shallow gardens of fast-growing, fast-withering seeds in his honor, and the quick blooming and swift death of these Adonis gardens enacted the fragile cycle of vegetation.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: When a Greek died, the soul travelled to the realm of Hades, and to enter it the shade had to cross the river Styx. The ferryman Charon waited on the bank, and he would carry only those who could pay his fee, a coin placed upon or beneath the tongue of the corpse before burial. The unburied and the penniless were turned away to wander the gloomy shore for a hundred years, which is why the Greeks regarded a proper burial as a sacred and absolute duty owed to the dead.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The legendary emperor Yu the Great earned his title by mastering the catastrophic floods that had drowned the early kingdom for generations. His father had tried and failed by building dams to block the waters and was executed for it. Yu chose instead to work with the flood rather than against it, dredging channels and digging canals to guide the water safely to the sea. The labor consumed thirteen years, during which Yu passed the door of his own home three times without once stepping inside to rest.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Oya is the Yoruba orisha of the wind, storms, and the river Niger, a warrior goddess and the companion of Shango. She commands the whirlwind and the lightning's gusting fury, and she stands as a guardian at the gateway between the living and the dead. The legends describe her as fierce and transformative, a force that sweeps away the old to clear ground for the new, and her devotees turn to her in times of upheaval and great change.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: The legend of Quetzalcoatl's promised return cast a long shadow over the history of Mexico. The Aztecs held that the feathered serpent would come back from the east in a particular year of their calendar, and the priest-king's prophecy of return was woven deeply into their sense of time and fate. When ships appeared from the eastern sea, some accounts say, the old legend stirred uneasily, and the myth of the homecoming god became entangled with the catastrophe of conquest.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Oshun is the Yoruba orisha of the river, of sweet waters, love, beauty, and fertility, and one important story places her at the center of the world's survival. When the male orishas tried to organize the world without including her, every effort they made failed and the rains would not come. Only when they begged Oshun's forgiveness and honored her did the fertilizing waters return. The tale taught that the gentle, life-giving power she embodied could not be dismissed without ruin.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: Across medieval Europe, the werewolf was a creature of dread, a person who by curse, witchcraft, or a pact with darkness took the form and hunger of a wolf. Some traditions held that a man became a werewolf by donning a belt of wolf-skin or by sleeping outdoors on a Friday under a full moon. Once transformed, the werewolf was driven to hunt and kill, and the only certain remedy was to wound the beast, for the same injury would appear on the human body and reveal the secret of its dual nature.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: The pilgrimage to the west gathered a strange company around the monk Xuanzang. Besides the Monkey King there was Zhu Bajie, the pig-spirit, a gluttonous and lustful figure expelled from heaven and reborn in a pig's body. There was Sha Wujing, the sand monk, a former heavenly general doing penance in a river. And there was the dragon prince transformed into the white horse that carried Xuanzang. Together this band of reformed monsters and a gentle monk journeyed through eighty-one ordeals.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The leshy is the lord of the forest in Slavic belief, a shapeshifting spirit who can stand as tall as the highest pine or shrink to the size of a blade of grass. He herds the wild animals as a farmer herds cattle, and he delights in leading travelers astray, twisting paths into circles and imitating familiar voices among the trees. A lost wanderer who suspected the leshy's mischief was advised to turn every garment inside out and put the left shoe on the right foot, confounding the spirit's trick.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: The frost giants of Jotunheim were ancient enemies of Thor, and the thunder god spent much of his strength upon their destruction. Yet not all of the jotnar were hostile. The giant Aegir brewed ale for the gods and hosted their feasts in his hall beneath the sea, and his wife Ran gathered the drowned into her net. The wise giant Mimir guarded a well of wisdom, and Odin sacrificed an eye to drink from it, a reminder that the giants held knowledge the gods needed.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: The siren of Greek myth was not the gentle mermaid of later imagination but a deadly creature, part woman and part bird, who perched on rocky islands and sang with irresistible sweetness. Their song lured sailors to steer toward the voice, and ship after ship was wrecked upon the reefs, the shore white with the bones of the dead. Odysseus, warned by the witch Circe, had his crew stop their ears with wax and bind him to the mast, so that he alone heard the song and survived to tell of it.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: The shimmering curtains of the aurora borealis were given many meanings in Arctic spirit tradition. Some Inuit groups believed the dancing lights were the spirits of the dead, playing a game with a walrus skull as their ball. Others held that the lights could be summoned by whistling, or warned that they were dangerous and might descend to carry off a careless onlooker. The night sky over the Arctic was not empty but populated, a place where the dead moved and watched.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: Apollo's loves were marked by loss. He loved Daphne, and she became a laurel tree to escape him. He loved the youth Hyacinthus, and a discus killed him. He loved the princess Coronis, and discovered her unfaithfulness through a white raven that had spied for him; in his grief and rage he killed her, then in fury scorched the raven black, and that, the Greeks said, is why ravens are no longer white. The bright god of poetry and prophecy was, again and again, unlucky in love.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: Thor and Loki journeyed to the stronghold of the giant Utgarda-Loki, who challenged them to a series of contests. Thor was given a drinking horn and could not empty it; he wrestled an old woman and was forced to one knee; he tried to lift a gray cat and managed only to raise one paw. Afterward Utgarda-Loki revealed the truth: the horn's end was joined to the sea, the old woman was old age itself, and the cat was the Midgard Serpent. Thor's failures had been magnificent.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: The duppy is the restless ghost of Jamaican and wider Caribbean folklore, the spirit of a dead person that lingers in the world to trouble the living. A duppy might be set upon an enemy by an obeah practitioner, or it might haunt the place of its burial of its own unquiet will. People guarded against duppies in many ways, scattering them with the smoke of certain herbs, hanging objects to confuse them, and burying the dead with care so the spirit would not feel cause to return.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: As Beowulf lay dying, he asked Wiglaf to bring out some of the dragon's treasure so that he might look upon it, and he gave thanks that he had won such a hoard for his people. He commanded that a great barrow be raised on a headland above the sea, a mound that sailors would see from afar and call Beowulf's Barrow. Then the old king died, the last of his line, and the loyal Wiglaf rebuked the warriors who had fled and left their lord to face the dragon nearly alone.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: Tezcatlipoca, the smoking mirror, was the dark and powerful god of night, sorcery, and destiny, an unpredictable deity who tempted, tested, and brought low both mortals and gods. He carried an obsidian mirror in place of one foot, said to have been bitten off by the earth monster, and in its black surface he could see all that happened in the world. His ancient rivalry with Quetzalcoatl shaped the myths, as the two gods alternately built up the worlds and tore them down.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The dragon takes profoundly different forms in the world's mythologies. In the imagination of medieval Europe it was a fire-breathing reptile, a hoarder of gold and a devourer of maidens, a monster to be slain by a saint or a knight. In China the dragon was its near opposite, a benevolent serpentine being of the rains and rivers, a bringer of fortune and a symbol of imperial power. The same word came to name two creatures whose meanings were almost reversed.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: Many remedies were used to keep the dead from rising in Balkan villages. A suspected corpse might be buried face down, so that if it tried to claw its way out it would dig itself deeper into the earth. Sharp objects, thorns, or sickles were placed in or around the grave. Some communities scattered seeds or grains of millet in the coffin, in the belief that the vampire would be compelled to count them one by one, an endless task that would keep it occupied until the safety of dawn.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: The islands of the Pacific were Maui's catch. Sailing far out with his brothers, he lowered a magic fishhook baited with blood from his own nose and felt a tremendous weight take hold. He chanted and strained until a great fish rose dripping from the depths, and that fish became the land. The North Island of New Zealand is still called Te Ika-a-Maui, the Fish of Maui, and the brothers' impatient hacking at it, before the proper rites were done, is why the island is rugged with mountains and valleys.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: Orpheus, the greatest of all musicians, descended into the underworld to reclaim his wife Eurydice, who had died of a serpent's bite. His music was so heartbreakingly beautiful that the wheel of Ixion stood still, the tormented dead forgot their pain, and even the iron heart of Hades was moved. The god granted Orpheus his wish, but on one condition: that he walk ahead of Eurydice toward the light and not look back at her until both had reached the world above.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: In the tale of Rumpelstiltskin, a miller's boastful lie traps his daughter, who is locked in a room and ordered by the king to spin straw into gold or die. A strange little man appears and spins the gold for her, taking a price each time, until at last he demands her firstborn child. He offers one escape: if she can guess his name within three days, the bargain is void. Only by chance does a messenger overhear the little man singing his own name by his fire in the forest.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: The founding myth of the Inca dynasty tells of Manco Capac and his sister-wife Mama Ocllo, children of the sun god, who emerged from the waters of Lake Titicaca. The sun sent them to find the place where a golden staff would sink into the earth, for there they were to build a great city. They wandered until they reached the fertile valley where the staff vanished into the rich soil, and on that spot they founded Cuzco, the navel of the Inca world.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Anansi heard of a magnificent feast and resolved to eat at every cooking pot in the village without missing a single one. He spun eight long threads, tied one end of each around his waist, and gave the other ends to eight people, instructing each to tug when the food was ready. But every pot finished at once, and all eight strands pulled at the same moment in eight directions. The threads cinched tight, squeezing the spider's once-broad body into the narrow, pinched shape it has worn ever since.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The vodyanoy was the malevolent water spirit of Slavic rivers and millponds, imagined as a bloated old man with a green beard, fish scales, and weeds tangled in his hair. He lurked beneath mill wheels and quiet pools, dragging swimmers and careless bathers to their deaths to swell the ranks of drowned souls who served him. Millers, whose livelihood depended on the water, treated him with wary respect and were rumored to offer him a black pig or a measure of grain to keep their wheels turning.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: The trickster of Native American tradition was never a simple villain. Coyote, Raven, Iktomi, and the others occupied a space between the sacred and the absurd, capable of creation and destruction in the same breath. They broke the rules so that listeners could see where the rules lay; they suffered the consequences of folly so that no one need suffer them in earnest. To tell a trickster tale was to teach without preaching, to bind a community together in shared laughter at a creature who was, in part, everyone.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: In Slavic folklore the vodyanitsa or vodyanoy's female counterpart, and in some regions a kind of rusalka, were the water maidens of rivers and lakes. The Germanic peoples told of the nixie, a water sprite who might appear as a beautiful woman combing her long hair by the water's edge or as a handsome man playing a fiddle. The nixie's music could draw the unwary into the deep, and parents warned their children that a friendly stranger met beside the river might not be human at all.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The Mahabharata centers on a dynastic struggle between two sets of cousins, the five virtuous Pandavas and the hundred Kauravas. Through a rigged game of dice, the eldest Pandava gambled away his kingdom, his brothers, and even their shared wife Draupadi. The attempt to publicly disrobe Draupadi in the assembly hall was halted only by a miracle, as her sari lengthened endlessly, and this humiliation set in motion a war that would consume nearly every warrior of an age.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The churning of the ocean of milk was a vast cooperative labor between the gods and the demons, who together sought the nectar of immortality hidden in the depths. They used the mountain Mandara as a churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope. As they pulled, the ocean yielded marvels and terrors alike: the wish-granting cow, the goddess Lakshmi, and a poison so deadly it threatened all creation, which the god Shiva drank and held forever in his throat, staining it blue.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: The fire giant Surtr would come from the burning south at Ragnarok, his flaming sword brighter than the sun. He would advance across the shattered rainbow bridge and onto the field of Vigrid, where the last battle was fought. After the gods had fallen, Surtr would fling fire across all the nine worlds, and the flames would consume Yggdrasil, the homes of gods and men alike, until the scorched earth sank at last beneath the boiling sea.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The gumiho is the nine-tailed fox of Korean folklore, a fox that has lived a thousand years and gained the power to take the shape of a beautiful woman. Unlike the kitsune of Japan, the gumiho of older Korean tales was almost always dangerous, a creature said to need human livers or hearts to survive. Some legends offered her a path to becoming fully human, often requiring her to abstain from killing for a thousand days, a test of restraint that the stories rarely allowed her to complete.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: When Grendel came to the hall of Heorot that night, Beowulf lay waiting. The monster seized one warrior and devoured him, then reached for Beowulf, and found his arm caught in a grip stronger than any he had ever known. Grendel writhed and pulled in terror to escape, but the hero would not let go, and at last the monster tore himself free only by leaving his whole arm and shoulder behind. Mortally wounded, Grendel fled to die in his marsh, and the hall rejoiced at the trophy hung beneath its roof.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: Folk belief in the Near East held that the very air was thick with unseen spirits, and the shedim were the demons of Jewish lore. They were said to dwell in ruined places, in deserts, and near water, and to be most active at night and at noon. The shedim could cause illness and madness, and a host of practices grew up to ward them off, from amulets and incantations to the custom of not greeting a stranger by a well or of pouring out the first water drawn in the morning.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The oni are the brutal ogres of Japanese myth, towering creatures with red or blue skin, wild hair, and horns, often clutching a spiked iron club called a kanabo. They burst from the gates of hell to punish the wicked and devour the unwary. Yet the festival of Setsubun turns the tables each year, when families fling roasted soybeans through their homes shouting that demons must leave and good fortune enter, driving the oni out with nothing more fearsome than a handful of beans.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: Medusa was once a beautiful maiden, but transformed into a monster with serpents for hair and a gaze that turned any living thing to stone. The hero Perseus was sent to claim her head, an errand meant to kill him. Armed with a mirrored shield from Athena, winged sandals, and a cap of invisibility, Perseus approached her looking only at her reflection, never directly. He struck while she slept, and from her severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus, born of her blood.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: The first man and woman, Ask and Embla, were shaped from two driftwood logs the gods found upon the shore. Odin gave them breath, Hoenir gave them sense and motion, and Lodur gave them warmth and the bloom of living color. Lifeless wood became thinking flesh, and from this pair every human generation descended, walking the middle realm of Midgard that the gods had ringed with the eyelashes of Ymir to keep the giants out.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The most agonizing episode of the Tain is the combat between Cu Chulainn and Ferdiad. The two had trained together as youths under the warrior-woman Scathach and loved one another as foster-brothers. Now Medb compelled Ferdiad to face the hero at the ford. For three days they fought and then tended each other's wounds and shared food across the water by night. On the fourth day Cu Chulainn was forced to use the dreadful barbed spear, the Gae Bolga, and Ferdiad fell, and the hero wept over the friend he had killed.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The legend of the each-uisge, the water horse of the Scottish Highlands, made it even more deadly than the lowland kelpie. The each-uisge lived in the sea and the deep lochs, and when it carried a victim into the water, it tore them apart and devoured everything but the liver, which floated to the surface. So feared was the creature that Highlanders were wary of any lone horse or pony found near the water, and would not touch a strange beast that might be the each-uisge wearing a gentle shape.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Shango, the orisha of thunder and lightning, was once, the legends say, a mortal king of the city of Oyo, a ruler of great power and a fearsome temper. After his reign ended in tragedy, he ascended and became the orisha of the storm. His devotees say that when lightning strikes, Shango has hurled a thunderstone to the earth, and the polished stone axes found in the soil are gathered as sacred objects, the very weapons cast down by the thunder god.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: Orpheus climbed the long dark path toward the daylight, listening for the footsteps of Eurydice behind him, but the underworld was silent and he heard nothing. As he stepped at last into the light, doubt overcame him, and he turned to see if she truly followed. She did, but she had not yet crossed the threshold, and at his glance she slipped backward into the dark with a final faint farewell. Orpheus had lost her a second time, and this time forever.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: Time ran differently in the Otherworld, and this was the cruelest of its enchantments. A man who spent what felt like a single evening dancing in a fairy ring might return to find his cottage gone, his family long dead, and his name a half-remembered story. Others vanished for a year and a day, the traditional span of fairy captivity, and came back unchanged while the world had moved on without them. The sidhe did not always mean harm; their gift of timelessness was simply not made for mortal lives.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The dwarf Vamana, fifth avatar of Vishnu, approached the generous demon king Bali and humbly begged for as much land as he could cover in three strides. Bali, amused by the small request, agreed. Then Vamana swelled into a cosmic giant. With his first step he spanned the entire earth, with his second the heavens, and finding nowhere left for the third, the king offered his own head. Vishnu pressed Bali down into the underworld, but honored his devotion by granting him kingship there.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Thor and the Midgard Serpent, ancient enemies, would meet for the last time at Ragnarok. The serpent Jormungandr, whose coiled body encircled the whole world, would rise from the sea spewing venom across the sky and water. Thor would battle the great snake and at last strike it dead with his hammer. But the thunder god would manage only nine steps from the serpent's corpse before the poison flooding his veins brought him down, and so the mightiest of the gods would die in his moment of victory.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The tale of Hansel and Gretel reflects the famine and hardship of old Europe in its grim opening: a poor woodcutter's family, unable to feed two children, abandons them in the forest. Lost among the trees, the children come upon a cottage built of bread and cake and sugar, the home of a cannibal witch who fattens Hansel for her oven. It is Gretel who saves them, tricking the witch into the oven she had prepared, and the children find their way home laden with the witch's treasure.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: Callisto was a nymph and a companion of the chaste goddess Artemis until Zeus deceived and seduced her. When her condition was discovered, she was banished from Artemis's band, and the jealous Hera transformed her into a bear. For years Callisto roamed the forest in that shape, until her own son, grown to be a hunter, came upon her and raised his spear. To prevent the unwitting matricide, Zeus swept them both into the sky, where they became the constellations of the Great Bear and the Little Bear.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: The river god Alpheus fell in love with the nymph Arethusa, a follower of the chaste Artemis, and pursued her relentlessly. To save her, Artemis transformed Arethusa into a stream, but Alpheus, undeterred, mingled his own waters with hers. The myth held that the stream of Arethusa traveled in secret beneath the sea all the way from Greece to the island of Sicily, where it surfaced as a freshwater spring, and that the waters of the river Alpheus still followed her even there.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: Grendel was given a name that the old tradition used for the outcast and the kin of monsters, and he was said to descend from Cain, the first murderer, cursed and exiled from the company of humankind. The monsters of the heroic tradition were not random horrors but figures of exile, envy, and the dark that lay outside the bonds of kinship and the gift-giving of the hall. Grendel hated the sound of the harp and the joy of men precisely because he was shut out from it forever.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: The Ramayana traveled across Southeast Asia and was reshaped by every culture it reached. In Thailand it became the Ramakien, the national epic, with Rama as the model of righteous kingship and the demon Tosakanth in the role of Ravana. In Indonesia and Malaysia it was performed in the shadow-puppet theater, the wayang kulit, where intricately carved leather figures cast their stories upon a lit screen through the night, and the heroes and demons of an ancient Indian tale became wholly local possessions.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: The Aztecs believed they lived in the age of the Fifth Sun, and that four worlds had been created and destroyed before it. The first sun was devoured by jaguars, the second swept away by hurricanes, the third consumed by a rain of fire, and the fourth drowned in a great flood that turned humankind into fish. Each destruction had reset the cosmos, and the current age too was destined to end, this time torn apart by earthquakes, a knowledge that gave Aztec religion its restless urgency.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: Inti, the sun god, was the most important deity of the Inca state and the divine ancestor from whom the ruling dynasty claimed descent. The great festival of Inti Raymi was held at the winter solstice, when the sun was at its weakest and farthest, and the people gathered at Cuzco to honor Inti and beg him to return and warm the land. The Inca ruler himself, called the son of the sun, presided over the rites that were meant to renew the bond between the people and the giver of light.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The false hero is a recurring villain of the wonder tale, the one who claims the credit and the reward that rightly belong to another. The true hero slays the dragon but is wounded or sleeping; an impostor finds the body, cuts off the dragon's heads, and carries them to the king to claim the princess. The tale builds to the moment of unmasking, when the real hero produces the dragon's tongues, hidden away as proof, and the false hero's lie collapses in the wedding hall.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Sphinx sat upon a rock outside Thebes and would not let any traveler pass unless they answered her riddle, devouring all who failed: what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening. Many died until Oedipus came and gave the answer, that it was a human being, who crawls as an infant, walks upright as an adult, and leans on a staff in old age. Defeated, the Sphinx threw herself from the rock to her death, and the road to Thebes was freed.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: The Kalevala was not an ancient text passed down whole, but a great epic assembled in the nineteenth century by the physician Elias Lonnrot. He travelled through the rural districts of Finland and Karelia, listening to elderly singers who still performed the old runic songs, the oral poetry of charms, origins, and heroes. Lonnrot collected, selected, and stitched these scattered songs into a continuous narrative, giving Finland a national epic drawn from a folk tradition that had survived only in living memory.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: Solomon, in folk tradition, was not only a wise king but a master of the spirit world. Legend held that he possessed a signet ring engraved with a divine name, and with it he could command the jinn and the demons, sealing the rebellious ones into brass vessels and casting them into the sea. The demons labored at his bidding, raising the Temple and revealing hidden knowledge, and Solomon's mastery over them became the seed of a vast later literature of magic and binding.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: In the beginning, the Greeks said, there was only Chaos, a yawning void. From it emerged Gaia, the broad-breasted earth, and Tartarus, the deep pit beneath, and Eros, the force of desire. Gaia brought forth Uranus, the starry sky, to cover her on every side, and from the union of earth and sky came the first generations of beings: the twelve Titans, the one-eyed Cyclopes, and the hundred-handed giants, the Hecatoncheires.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: The Tuatha De Danann, the divine race of Irish myth, did not vanish when the mortal Milesians conquered Ireland. Instead they withdrew into the Otherworld, the realm beneath the green hills and ancient burial mounds called sidhe. From these earthen palaces they became the aos si, the fairy folk, neither gods nor ghosts but a separate people living alongside the human world, glimpsed at twilight and feared at the turning festivals of the year.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: At the end of the long journey, the pilgrims reached the Buddha's paradise in the west and received the sacred scriptures, and for their faithfulness through eighty-one ordeals each was rewarded. The monk Xuanzang and the Monkey King were both elevated to the rank of Buddha; the pig and the sand monk were given holy posts; the dragon-horse became a true dragon again. The golden band that had bound Sun Wukong to obedience vanished from his head, for he no longer needed it.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: Inuit tradition told of the adlet, beings born of the union of a woman and a great dog, half human and half hound. The story explained the origin of certain feared peoples and of dog-kind itself, for the woman set some of her strange children adrift in a boot or a vessel and sent the rest inland. The tale, like much Arctic folklore, used the figures of animals and spirits to explain the shape of the world, the kinds of beings in it, and the uneasy boundaries between them.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Nemean Lion, the Erymanthian Boar, the Stymphalian Birds, and the Cretan Bull were among the monsters set against Heracles in his labors, but the strangest of his foes was the giant Antaeus. Antaeus challenged all travelers to wrestle and was invincible, for he drew renewed strength each time he touched his mother, the Earth. Heracles discovered the secret, lifted the giant clear off the ground, and held him aloft, cut off from his source of power, until the strength drained from his body.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: Loki fathered three monstrous children upon the giantess Angrboda, and when the gods learned of them and the prophecies of doom that surrounded them, they resolved to act. They cast the great serpent Jormungandr into the ocean encircling the world, where it grew until it could bite its own tail. They flung the death-goddess Hel down into the underworld to rule the dishonored dead. And the wolf Fenrir they kept among themselves, trying to bind him, until the danger forced a crueler measure.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The legend of the brownie belonged to the farms and houses of the Scottish lowlands and borders. The brownie was a small, rough, hairy spirit attached to a household, who came out at night to thresh the grain, sweep the floors, and finish the work the family had left undone. The brownie asked nothing but a bowl of cream or fresh bread set out for him. He must never be paid with clothing or thanked too openly, for an offered gift would offend him, and the affronted brownie would depart and never return.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The youngest of three is the favored hero of countless European tales, the despised or underestimated child who succeeds where the elder siblings fail. The two older brothers ride out first, scorn the small creature who asks for help, and come to grief. The youngest shares his last crust of bread with the old woman or the talking fox, and his kindness is repaid with the magic that wins the prize. The tales insist, against the order of the world, that the last shall be first.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The legend of Naupaka explains the strange flower of the Hawaiian shores, a bloom that looks as if it has been torn in half. The tale tells of two lovers separated by fate or by rank, one bound to the mountains and one to the sea. In her grief one of them tore a flower in two, keeping half and giving half to her beloved. Ever since, the naupaka of the mountains and the naupaka of the beach each bear only half a flower, and the legend says they will be whole only when the lovers are reunited.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: Among the spirit-beings feared in Inuit folklore was the qalupalik, a creature of the sea that lived beneath the ice. It was said to have green skin, long hair, and long fingernails, and it carried a pouch on its back called an amautik. The qalupalik would hum near the shore and the breathing holes, waiting to snatch children who wandered too close to the dangerous ice without their parents. The legend kept the young safely back from the deadly edges of the frozen sea.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: Hawaiian tradition speaks of the aumakua, ancestral guardian spirits that watch over a family across the generations. An aumakua might take the form of a shark, an owl, a hawk, a turtle, or another creature, and a family that recognized a shark as its aumakua would never harm one and might be protected by it in the water. The aumakua bridged the living and the dead, the ancestors continuing to guide and guard their descendants through the body of a chosen animal.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The Lorelei is a steep rock on the bank of the Rhine, and German legend gave it an enchantress. A beautiful maiden was said to sit upon the rock, combing her golden hair and singing a song of unearthly sweetness. The boatmen who navigated the swift and narrow waters below would look up, entranced by her song and her beauty, and lose their attention to the dangerous current, and so their boats were dashed upon the rocks and the sailors drowned beneath the singing of the Lorelei.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: Cu Chulainn, the great hero of the Ulster Cycle, was born Setanta and earned his name as a boy. Invited to a feast at the house of the smith Culann, the child arrived late, and the smith's monstrous guard hound attacked him. Setanta killed the beast with his bare hands, or by driving a hurling ball down its throat. To make amends, the boy offered to guard the smith's house himself until a new hound was reared, and so he became Cu Chulainn, the Hound of Culann.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: The Inca told that the creator god Viracocha rose from the depths of Lake Titicaca to make the world. He first fashioned a race of beings, but displeased with them, he destroyed them in a great flood and turned others to stone. Then Viracocha made the sun, the moon, and the stars, and a new humankind, painting each nation with its own dress and language and customs. His work done, the creator walked across the land teaching, and at last departed across the western ocean, promising one day to return.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The grateful animal is among the most beloved helpers of the European wonder tale. The hero, traveling toward the great task, comes upon a fish stranded out of water, an ant beneath a careless foot, an eagle caught in a snare. Where the cruel brothers would pass by or do harm, the true hero stops to help, asking nothing. Later, at the moment of greatest need, the saved creature returns, and the small mercy shown in passing turns out to have been the whole secret of the hero's success.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The mo'o were the great water lizards or dragon-spirits of Hawaiian legend, vast reptilian beings, often female, who guarded fishponds, pools, and the freshwater places of the islands. A mo'o could be a fearsome guardian or a protective family aumakua, and a pool watched by one was a place to approach with care and respect. The mo'o belonged to the deep, still water, and their presence marked the boundary between the safe human shore and the powerful, watchful world beneath the surface.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: In a story told among the peoples of the Pacific Northwest, the world lay in darkness because a selfish chief kept the sun, moon, and stars locked in carved boxes in his lodge. Raven, the trickster, transformed himself into a tiny hemlock needle, floated into the drinking water, and was swallowed by the chief's daughter, who gave birth to him as a child. Raven the infant cried and cried for the boxes until the doting grandfather opened them, and the trickster, seizing the light, became a bird again and flew it up into the sky.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The folklore of the evil eye was deeply woven into the cultures of the Near East and the Mediterranean. It was believed that a glance of envy or admiration, even unintended, could carry a harmful power that brought sickness, accident, or ruin upon its object. Children, livestock, and new ventures were thought especially vulnerable. Blue beads, the open-palmed hamsa, recited blessings, and a pinch of salt were all used to absorb, deflect, or break the malign power of the watching eye.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: The merrow was the mermaid of Irish folklore, and unlike many water spirits she was often gentle toward humankind. The merrow wore a magic cap, the cohuleen druith, which allowed her to travel through the water, and a man who found and hid the cap could keep a merrow ashore as his bride. Yet the sea always called to her, and like the selkie wife of Scotland, the merrow who recovered her cap would slip back beneath the waves, leaving her human family behind.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: The world of Beowulf is one in which monsters press always at the edges of the lighted hall. Grendel comes out of the dark fen, his mother from the haunted mere, the dragon from the ancient barrow. The hall, with its fire and its fellowship and its songs, is a fragile circle of human warmth, and the hero is the one who steps out of that circle into the darkness to hold the monsters back. The poem knows that the holding cannot last forever, and that every hall will fall in its time.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The bear-woman of the founding legend, called Ungnyeo, longed for a child, and Hwanung, moved by her devotion, took human form and married her. Their son was Dangun, who is said to have founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon, in ancient times and to have ruled it for many centuries before withdrawing to become a mountain god. Koreans long honored Dangun as the legendary ancestor of their nation, the human child of a heavenly god and a bear who had willed herself into a woman.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: Zeus was raised in secret on the island of Crete, hidden from his father in a cave and nourished by a divine goat. When he came to manhood, he returned to confront Cronus, and with a potion he forced the Titan to vomit up the children he had swallowed: Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon, all emerging fully grown, along with the stone that had been swallowed in Zeus's place. The freed gods rallied to their brother, and the war for the cosmos began.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: Gilgamesh crossed the waters of death to reach Utnapishtim, the only mortal granted everlasting life, hoping to learn how he too might escape the grave. The flood survivor set him a simple test: to conquer death, first conquer sleep, and stay awake for six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh failed at once, slumbering where he sat, and a loaf of bread baked fresh each day was laid beside him to count his shame. He could not even master sleep, the small brother of death.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: The saga of the Volsungs gave the Germanic world one of its most enduring stories, and it survived in many forms. The same essential tale of the dragon-slayer, the cursed treasure, the betrayed valkyrie, and the doomed royal house appears in the German Nibelungenlied, where the hero is called Siegfried. The story carried the old conviction that fate is inescapable, that a curse once spoken runs its course, and that even the bravest hero is only a thread in a pattern already woven.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: Persephone, daughter of the harvest goddess Demeter, was gathering flowers in a meadow when the earth split open and Hades carried her down to be his queen. Demeter's grief was so terrible that the crops withered and famine threatened the world. Zeus commanded Persephone's return, but because she had eaten a few pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she was bound to it. The compromise gave her to her mother for part of the year and to Hades for the rest, and her annual descent became the coming of winter.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: When the battle-fury, the riastrad or warp-spasm, came upon Cu Chulainn, his body contorted into a monstrous and unrecognizable shape. His muscles bulged, one eye sank into his skull and the other started out upon his cheek, his hair stood stiff with a drop of blood at each tip, and a great spout of dark blood, the hero-light, rose from the crown of his head. In this terrible transformed state he was a danger to friend and foe alike, and after the battle the men of Ulster had to plunge him into vats of cold water to cool his rage.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The founding of Rome began with a crime and a betrayal. The twin brothers Romulus and Remus were sons of the war god Mars and a Vestal Virgin, and a fearful king ordered them drowned in the Tiber. The basket carrying them washed ashore, and a she-wolf found the infants and suckled them at her den until a shepherd took them in. Raised to manhood unaware of their royal blood, the twins would grow up to overthrow the usurper and resolve to build a city of their own.
